title: The Party

source.quote: there are six different ways in which they can spend their time

setting: Camellia's housewarming party, 9 p.m. Six little clusters have formed around the apartment, and each one is doing something different with the next twenty minutes.

L1.line: Rosita, mid-conversation with two others: "I did a group like this before - we never did figure out what it was for either." The other two nod and trade their own old stories. Nobody suggests doing anything about tonight.
cues: talking about 'back when', not about tonight
L1.question: Three people are trading stories about past groups and parties, going nowhere in particular. What's this corner doing?

options.text: Activity - they're working something out together.
options.feedback: Activity is goal-directed, aimed at a material outcome. Nobody here is trying to produce anything; they're just talking about what happened before.

options.text: Pastime - familiar talk about something, with no one proposing to do anything about it.
options.feedback: Right. "Pastime = past time": comfortable, structured chat about a shared topic that goes nowhere, which is exactly what sets it apart from activity.

options.text: Game - someone's about to get a bad feeling out of this.
options.feedback: No ulterior transactions here, no switch, no bad-feeling payoff - just low-stakes shared talk. That's a pastime, not a game.

options.text: Intimacy - they're being completely open with each other.
options.feedback: Intimacy requires authentic, uncensored feelings and wants exchanged directly; swapping old party stories is far more guarded and routine than that.

L1.lesson: Pastiming is light, familiar talk about a shared subject with no commitment to act on it - the giveaway is 'pastime = past time,' people recounting what already happened rather than doing anything now. Confusing it with activity misses that nothing here is aimed at a material outcome; confusing it with a game misses that nobody's heading toward a bad-feeling payoff.

L2.intro: Mike moves through the apartment. Five more corners, five more ways of structuring the same twenty minutes.

beats.line: He's standing near the window with a drink, eyes somewhere out past the balcony, not looking at anyone.
cues: physically present, not transacting with anyone

options.text: Walk over and ask what he's thinking about, direct and warm.
options.outcome: Arjun blinks, like coming back from somewhere. "Oh - sorry, just drifted off. I'm okay, just needed a minute." He rejoins the room.
options.lesson: Withdrawal only produces self-strokes; a direct, low-pressure check-in is often enough of an invitation back in, without demanding he perform sociability he doesn't have energy for.

options.text: Leave him alone - he probably wants space.
options.outcome: Mike moves on. Arjun stays at the window for another twenty minutes, undisturbed and unstroked.
options.lesson: Respecting withdrawal is reasonable, but it's worth remembering that withdrawing only refills the stroke bank from self-strokes, which is never a full replacement for strokes from other people.

options.text: Announce to the room: "Hey, somebody go cheer up Arjun, he looks miserable over there."
options.outcome: Arjun stiffens, embarrassed, and now has an audience for a feeling he hadn't even named yet.
options.lesson: Narrating someone's internal state to the room turns quiet withdrawal into a public diagnosis nobody asked for - and diagnosing ego state from the outside is exactly what you can't reliably do during withdrawal, which is why it often can't be confirmed by the people watching.

beats.line: Troy's shaking hands with each new arrival: "Hey! Good to see you! Come on in!" - same four words, same handshake, four times running.

options.text: Match it - same handshake, same warm four words, when it's your turn to be greeted.
options.outcome: It's seamless. Mike's in the door and in the party in under five seconds, exactly as intended.
options.lesson: A ritual's entire value is its predictability - matching the expected exchange pays the stroke it's designed to pay, cleanly and fast, which is the point.

options.text: Try to turn the doorway greeting into a real conversation about your week.
options.outcome: Troy looks faintly thrown, half-listens while glancing at the next arrival over Mike's shoulder, then repeats his line to them too.
options.lesson: A ritual slot is sized for a ritual; pouring something bigger into it doesn't get received, it just creates a mismatch - that something bigger belongs in pastime or intimacy, not the doorway handshake.

options.text: Walk past without shaking his offered hand.
options.outcome: Troy's hand hangs there a second too long. He doesn't say anything, but he notices.
options.lesson: Ignoring an offered ritual stroke isn't neutral - ritual participants keep a close count, so a skipped handshake registers as a real, if small, negative.

beats.line: Camellia's elbow-deep in the sink: "If you actually want to help, the glasses go on the left, the plates stack here - otherwise just stay out of the splash zone."

options.text: Grab a towel and start drying exactly where she pointed.
options.outcome: The counter clears in minutes. Camellia says, "Oh - thank you, actually," sounding surprised and genuinely pleased.
options.lesson: Activity is goal-directed, and its strokes come at the end, for the outcome - "thank you, actually" is a delayed conditional stroke for a job done, not idle chat.

options.text: Stand in the doorway chatting about the party while she washes alone.
options.outcome: Camellia keeps washing. The conversation is pleasant pastime, but the dishes don't move any faster.
options.lesson: Pastime and activity can happen side by side, but only one of them gets the dishes done - don't mistake friendly talk near a task for contributing to it.

options.text: Take over without asking and rearrange the kitchen "more efficiently."
options.outcome: Camellia's jaw tightens. "That's not where any of this goes." Now she's redoing Mike's "help."
options.lesson: Activity strokes are conditional on actually meeting the goal as defined - substituting your own goal for hers doesn't earn the stroke, it just creates more work.

beats.line: Dev says, "I just can't do anything right tonight, can I," with a little laugh, after spilling a drink nobody was upset about.
cues: fishing for a reaction before anyone's reacted

options.text: Say plainly: "It's a spilled drink, Dev, nobody's mad," and change the subject.
options.outcome: Dev blinks, a little deflated, then actually laughs for real. "Fair. Okay." The moment passes without anyone needing to rescue or scold him.
options.lesson: Declining the invitation - not rescuing, not scolding - avoids completing the switch; naming the actual situation from Adult crosses the ulterior invitation instead of answering it.

options.text: Rush to reassure him: "Oh no, you're fine, you're always so clumsy, it's endearing!"
options.outcome: Dev soaks it up - and five minutes later does something else self-deprecating, fishing for the same reassurance again.
options.lesson: Playing the expected comforting role completes the invitation he put out - it feels kind, but it's the complementary move that keeps this particular exchange running.

options.text: Say, half-joking, "Yeah, you kind of are a mess tonight."
options.outcome: Dev's face falls for real, then he laughs it off too quickly. Something about the room cools for a second nobody can quite name.
options.lesson: Taking the bait completes the switch - a sudden, mutual sense of 'what just happened,' right before the bad feelings land for both of you, is the tell that a game just played out.

beats.line: Priya, quietly, not performing it for anyone: "I've been dreading tonight. I didn't want to come alone. I'm really glad you're out here."
cues: no joke softening it, no hidden ask under it

options.text: Match it: "I'm glad too - I almost didn't come either." Stay with her instead of changing the subject.
options.outcome: Neither of them says anything for a second. It's comfortable, not awkward. The rest of the party feels easier after that.
options.lesson: Berne's own description of intimacy is specific: a candid Child-to-Child exchange set up by the Adult - straight feelings, no hidden agenda, no discount of what the other person just said.

options.text: Deflect with a joke to lighten the mood.
options.outcome: Priya laughs along, but something closes slightly in her face. The real thing she said doesn't get a real answer.
options.lesson: A joke here isn't dishonest, but it declines the invitation to intimacy - trading the one time-structure with no discounting for one that's easier precisely because it's lighter.

options.text: Say, "Oh, don't be dramatic, everyone loves a party!"
options.outcome: Priya's face shuts down. "Yeah. Sure. Never mind." She doesn't say anything else real for the rest of the night.
options.lesson: This discounts what she actually said instead of answering it - and discounting is specifically what intimacy, by definition, doesn't include; it turns a straight exchange into something closer to a small rejection.

fields.label: Draw the vectors for Troy's doorway ritual, and for the moment on the balcony with Priya.
In under 50 words: why can the same six people, at the same party, be in six different time-structures within twenty minutes of each other?

echo.setting: 48 hours later: a family group chat lights up.
echo.line: [12 new messages about nothing in particular]
echo.shape: same six-way sort, applied to a group chat instead of a party
